brief.head: The Nordic exception
brief.text: Scandinavia’s welfare states do not refute free markets, Amit Varma said. Those countries grew rich as free markets first, and could afford welfare statism only afterwards. {010-C16}

brief.head: Nobody designed it
brief.text: Languages, economies and natural selection need no central planner, Amit Varma said. They are, in Adam Ferguson’s words, “the products of human action and not human design”. {010-J15}

brief.head: Discovery, not design
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s phrase is “discovery, not design”. Poverty has never been ended by central planners, only by searchers who learn by trial and error, Amit Varma read from William Easterly. {010-C04}

brief.head: Two speeches a week
brief.text: At the finance ministry, Ajay Shah recalled, every joint secretary gave two conference speeches a week, to show business a capable crew with a vision and a strategy. {010-S10}

brief.head: Not about skin colour
brief.text: Indians once believed “because our skins are brown we’ll never be able to export”, Ajay Shah said. Manmohan Singh’s PhD thesis argued it was about incentives, prices and exchange rates. {010-C10}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why freedom matters
lead.head: Midnight’s unfree children
body: Amit Varma began by accounting for the cat. A young cat was mewing in the background, he explained, and it sounded “like the wailing of all the dispossessed and the hungry and the starving through these many, many years of India’s tormented journey”. {010-J01}
India ejected colonial rule in 1947, Ajay Shah said, but in many ways freedom did not then come to the people. “We ended up with less freedom in many respects.”
Varma agreed. He has long called the unfinished work India’s second freedom struggle.
## Consent and its fruits

Varma’s case rests on consent. “How should I live in this world?” and “how should the state relate to society?” look like separate questions, he said, but they share an answer: “consent is everything and coercion is the ultimate evil.” {010-C01}

Freedom, he argued, is also the road to prosperity. Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off, so the world is not zero-sum. Citing their friend Nitin Pai, he said that after 1991 each percentage point of GDP growth lifted three million Indians out of poverty.

Shah added that people can survive unfreedom, even in a concentration camp, but a society without agency stops creating. A poor country, he said, needs “an effervescence of optimism, of creativity, of invention”.
## Booms, busts and a near miss
Shah then walked through India’s history. Its share of pre-industrial world GDP, he said, reflected good weather and many people, not riches: “It was not a golden age.”

Modern India, in his telling, began around 1869, when the Suez Canal, the telegraph, the railway and British company law arrived almost at once. Wars, the Depression and Partition darkened the years from 1913 to 1947.
After Independence the numbers looked decent, but policy got steadily worse. Controls crept in, and each failure was met with more of them.
Shah recalled the audacity of 1947: universal suffrage in a country where women’s literacy was six per cent. {010-S05}

Between 1962 and 1977 the experiment nearly failed. Three wars, Nehru’s death, droughts, bank nationalisation, double-digit inflation and the Emergency left many fearing India would become “another disgusting authoritarian third world country”.
Varma, reading from Shruti Rajagopalan’s essay on those years, cited a top income-tax rate of 97.75 per cent. He thinks the economic controls did more harm than the Emergency.

Recovery began in 1977 under the Janata government, and Shah said careful econometrics dates the acceleration of growth to 1979. Varma noted that the reformers of 1991 had been preparing for a decade and a half.
## The fragile years
By 2011 the momentum had gone. Shah’s summary statistic: there was less freedom in 2010 than in 2000, and less in 2020 than in 2010.

Varma traced the slide to a chain of accidents after the Mumbai attacks of 2008. Shah found bad luck “a deeply dissatisfying solution”. The reformers, he said, had operated the old machinery of government more sensibly but never rebuilt it.
“What was keeping the ship aloft were certain individuals,” he said, “which to me is an unacceptable and fragile way of building a country.” {010-C13}

Varma confessed to growing despondent. Shah urged caution, not despair. Bright dawns in China, Russia and Weimar Germany turned ugly, he said, but post-war Germany and Japan became “beautiful countries”.
“The world is a rich and wonderful place,” he said, “and progress can always happen.” {010-C15}

second.label: The world before 1914
second.head: No papers, no problem
second.deck: Ajay Shah on freedoms lost to war, and never given back
body: Before 1914, Ajay Shah said, nobody anywhere in the world needed a passport. Royals wrote to each other asking favours for their friends, but ordinary people simply travelled and migrated. {010-S04}

Capital controls did not exist until Adolf Hitler introduced them in Germany. In India, curbs on trade and capital flows began as a British wartime measure in 1939. “The loss of freedom began as wartime measures,” Shah said, and has since been normalised.

The Treaty of Versailles had a clause restoring passport-free travel, and conferences pursued it into the 1960s. Soviet Russia blocked every attempt, because it never wanted its people to leave. Only the European Union has partly restored the old freedom. {010-J04}

quote.text: Did you know that before 1914 there were no passports anywhere in the world?

second.caption: the world before passports

third.head: Malaria’s cold comfort
body: Malaria was a huge problem in India, Amit Varma said, and the defence against it was quinine. {#malaria}
Quinine could not be had on its own: it was bitter and ugly. So it was put into tonic water, and gin and tonic became a popular cocktail in India. A gin and tonic needs ice.
This was the 19th century. “No fridges,” Varma said. “Where will the ice come from? America will make the ice.” And so a bunch of ice factories were set up in the American Midwest. {010-S02}

He offered it as a companion to Ajay Shah’s story of the American Civil War, which cut off cotton to Britain and created a new trade through Bombay. A disease in India built an industry across the world. “So the wonders of global capitalism,” Varma said.
third.caption: gin, tonic and American ice

p2.title: India’s second freedom
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah trace India’s economic history, from the Suez Canal to the lost decade

sections.label: The first principle
sections.head: Consent is everything
sections.caption: freedom as consent
body: Freedom is such a misused word that Amit Varma prefers to think in terms of consent. How should I live, and how should the state relate to society? One question seems to belong to ethics and the other to political philosophy, he said, but both have the same answer. {010-C01}

You can reach it from first principles, through individual autonomy and John Locke’s right to self-ownership, or from consequences, because freedom gives the best outcomes. Varma also flagged what he calls the grand liberal paradox: to enjoy our rights we need a state, and the state takes some of them away.
## Not a fixed pie

Our brains, he suggested, evolved in small tribes in times of scarcity, so we think in zero-sum terms. Angus Maddison’s chart of world GDP tells another story: it shoots up around 1800. The reason, Varma said, is that every voluntary transaction leaves both people better off, so the more of them there are, the richer the world becomes. {010-C02}

That makes freedom a humanitarian cause: he credited the 1991 reforms with bringing 300 to 400 million people out of poverty. Yet about 70 per cent of India was born after the Berlin Wall fell, and the young have forgotten the horrors of socialism. {#berlin}
~ Ajay Shah added what unfreedom costs. People survive it, even in a concentration camp, but once agency is taken away, the arts, science and business sink into “a dull despondence”.

quote.text: The answer is consent. That consent is everything and coercion is the ultimate evil.

sections.label: Before 1947
sections.head: A golden age that wasn’t
sections.caption: India before Independence
body: India’s large share of world GDP before industrialisation is no cause for nostalgia, Ajay Shah said. It reflected good weather and a big population, and output per person was abysmal everywhere. Old India had “very little political development” and “no rule of law”. {010-C06}

Modernity came, in his account, in the 1860s and 1870s, and it lasted until 1913. Then came a long dark period: two world wars, the Great Depression, the unrest of the freedom movement and the horrors of Partition, with British policies often hostile to the Indian economy.
## A return, not a rupture

Amit Varma read from the historian Tirthankar Roy’s essay: the empire created an economy open to trade, capital flows and settlement, and economic nationalists misread payments to Britain as a “drain” when they were the price of tapping a mobile market for skills and capital.
Varma also relayed an argument from Vinay Sitapati: 1991 should be seen as a re-liberalisation, because it was Nehru’s Fabian socialism and central planning that broke with the past. {010-C07}
~ Sitapati draws too on Richard Eaton’s *India in the Persianate Age*, which suggests that global trade moved power to the port cities and weakened the centralised empire. {010-R07}

quote.text: We should think of the liberalisation of ninety one as a re-liberalisation of ninety one.

sections.label: 1947 to 1962
sections.head: An empty seat for Laski
sections.caption: the planners of 1947
body: India in 1947 was freer than its later history suggests, Ajay Shah said. State intervention was modest, the level of freedom was relatively high, and “we’ve never had a better civil service in India than was present in 1947”. {010-S03}
Then, day after day, restrictions crept in. Amit Varma traced the mindset behind them. Nehru told J.R.D. Tata: “Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.” {010-J09}

A 1951 *Time* magazine piece called Beatrice and Sidney Webb, the godparents of Fabian socialism, “in a truer sense his creators than Vishnu and Shiva”. A wit quoted by Ramachandra Guha said that at every cabinet meeting “there was an empty seat and Harold Laski sat on it”. {010-J11}
## Wrong, and staying wrong

Varma saw three centralising impulses in 1947: political, as the country seemed to fall apart; social, as Ambedkar saw villages as dens of localism; and economic, in Nehru’s distrust of profit. The mistake, he said, was believing a liberal society could be imposed from the top down. {010-C08}

~ Shah’s complaint was not that the planners were wrong but that they would not change course. Some of the smartest people available answered every failure with more controls, insisting that “the floggings will continue until the morale improves”.

quote.text: It is okay to be wrong. It is not okay to be impervious to the evidence.

sections.label: 1962 to 1977
sections.head: Fifteen years on the brink
sections.caption: the terrifying years
body: India in 1947 was “a precocious political project”, Ajay Shah said: universal suffrage in a country where women’s literacy was six per cent. {010-S05}

Then came the China war of 1962, Nehru’s death in 1964, war with Pakistan in 1965, two droughts in a row, famine, and begging the United States for PL 480 food aid. The banks were nationalised in 1969. The 1971 war was “a nationalist wet dream”, he said, but an enormous economic burden.

The euphoria of the Bangladesh war and Indira Gandhi’s big election win gave way to double-digit inflation, the JP agitation and the Emergency. She was, Shah noted, the first Indian prime minister whom political scientists classify as a populist.
## Worse than the Emergency
Amit Varma, quoting Shruti Rajagopalan, listed tariffs above 350 per cent on some goods and the nationalisation of the 14 largest banks. The top income-tax rate was 97.75 per cent. {#tax}
Indira did not even believe in this socialism, Varma argued; she used it to tilt left against the syndicate. Her economic regulations, he said, were far worse than the Emergency. {#worse}
~ Democracy survived partly through embarrassment. Leaked diplomatic material, Shah said, shows Indira was embarrassed about the Emergency, and the 1977 elections were truly free and fair. {010-S07}

quote.text: It was only Sanjay Gandhi’s mother who could have declared the emergency, and it was only Jawaharlal Nehru’s daughter who could have declared elections.

sections.label: 1977 onwards
sections.head: Three Gujaratis turn the ship
sections.caption: the long road to 1991
body: In 1977 the Janata Party put three Gujaratis in charge: Morarji Desai as prime minister, H.M. Patel as finance minister and D.T. Lakdawala as deputy chairman of the Planning Commission. They were not radical reformers, Ajay Shah said, but they had an instinct for markets.

Lakdawala had always been at Bombay University, far from Delhi’s leftist economics establishment, and Patel had grown up near Amul and the cooperative movement. Small measures and key staffing choices began “a gentle process of turning the ship”.
Growth, Shah argued, comes only from the private sector committing its hours, its children and its money to building firms, and it does so when it feels safe about where India is heading. {010-C11}
The mood turned quickly: careful econometrics dates India’s growth acceleration to 1979. {#growth1979}
## Bug reports and landmines

From 1991 to 2011, Shah said, the state was full of landmines, but businesses that hit one could “file a bug report” and often get it fixed. That compact among India’s four elites broke down as the state’s deeds fell short of its words. {010-C12}

~ The reformers, he said, had run an old, repressive apparatus without rebuilding it. His counterexample was the United States under Donald Trump, where much of government worked as usual: “That is institutional quality.”

quote.text: Always and always and always there is only one source of economic growth and that is the private sector.

side.boxText: Around 2008 Amit Varma pitched *Freedom After Midnight* to the New India Foundation, arguing that 1947 brought only political freedom, not personal, social or economic freedom. He never wrote it “because I’m a lazy bum”, and the proposal was rejected anyway. {010-J02}

contQuote.text: People should not ask for fate to step out of the page of history and shake your hand. People should just be quiet and dig in and work hard and you have no right to ask for any reward.

stories.end: the technological capability of the Industrial Revolution was seeded into India all at once
stories.caption: the year India was wired in
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the decade that wired India to the world
stories.head: The short cut to modernity
body: Modern India did not begin in 1947, or in 1991, in Ajay Shah’s telling. It began in the 1860s and 1870s, and above all in 1869.

That year the Suez Canal started working, and the distance between London and Bombay came down dramatically. {#suez} Before it, a ship from London went around the Cape of Good Hope, and having come that far might as well carry on to Calcutta. After it, the route ran through the Straits of Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, “and boom, you are at Bombay”.

The telegraph arrived too. When the first connections reached Bombay in the 1860s, a message took about four hours between the two cities, so that cotton speculators could talk to each other. {#telegraph}

So did the railroad, and so did the legal plumbing of a market economy. The Companies Act, the Contract Act and the Evidence Act all came to India; the Companies Act reached Bombay within a couple of years of passing in London. In 1874 came the Bombay Stock Exchange. {#bse}
Then the American Civil War cut off cotton supplies from America to Britain. A whole cotton trade was invented in India: grown in Gujarat and Maharashtra, shipped through Bombay to London.
“It’s like the entire institutional package and the technological capability of the Industrial Revolution was seeded into India all at once,” Shah said. {010-S01}

~ This first modernisation, which coincides with what is called the first globalisation, ran roughly from 1869 to 1913. Shah thinks it goes unrecognised in India, not least because the nationalists oversold their case.
stories.why: Modern India is older than its usual birthdays. Connectivity, technology and the institutions of a market economy arrived together in a single burst, and the Indian economy had an explosive moment, until wars and the Depression closed the world again.
stories.postscript: He does not pine for colonial rule, Shah said. But history should be read “cold and clear”.

stories.caption: booking a scooter for a wedding
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the economics of the Indira years
stories.head: The bride wore a waiting list
body: By the time Indira Gandhi took office, Amit Varma read from Shruti Rajagopalan’s essay, the official goal was to nationalise all means of production. Her government nationalised the 14 largest banks overnight by ordinance, along with coal and copper mines and general insurance.
Some goods faced import tariffs above 350 per cent. The top income-tax rate was 97.75 per cent. {#tax} By the late 1970s it was almost impossible to start a business, or to exit a failing one.
Scarcity bred jokes. Parents of a girl were told to book a scooter early, so that it would be delivered by the time of her wedding. {010-S06}

~ Varma thinks Indira did not even believe in this socialism, and that her economic regulations kept millions in poverty for decades longer than necessary, stopping a labour-intensive manufacturing boom that could have come before China’s.

quote.text: India was the one country in the world where a secondhand car cost more than a new car.

stories.start: So I want to show two periods which are really inspiring
stories.end: for all you knew, the Indian project was going to crash
stories.caption: the reformers who came home
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the reformers who dug in
stories.head: Sharpening axes in the dark
body: Ajay Shah sees two dark stretches in modern Indian history. From 1927 to 1947 the British Empire looked infinitely powerful, yet the best Indians dug in, wrote longhand letters and argued about what India should be.
From 1962 to 1977 the same story played out. Shah was born in 1966 and has heard about those years from his elders. {#born1966} Many people gave up and left the country.

Manmohan Singh came home after his PhD with no promise that he would be finance minister or prime minister. “Nobody would have bet on a million to one odds that this was going to happen,” Shah said. {010-S09}
~ Montek Singh Ahluwalia, Amit Varma added, left the World Bank when Singh asked him to come back. Vijay Kelkar, Shah said, “just felt obliged to say, Yes, sir, I will,” and packed his bags.
stories.why: Big reforms rest on years of unrewarded preparation by people who chose to stay. Varma reached for Abraham Lincoln’s line: with six hours to cut a tree, spend the first five sharpening the axe. {010-J14}
stories.postscript: Just as we remember those who fought, Varma said, we should remember those who did not. Most people, Shah replied, were simply appeasers.

stories.caption: the attack that emptied a ministry
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how a terror attack derailed the economy
stories.head: Home calls, Finance empties
body: In 2008-09, Amit Varma said, everything was going well. Manmohan Singh was prime minister, P. Chidambaram was finance minister, and India was handling the global financial crisis capably. Then came the terrorist attacks on Mumbai.

The home minister, Shivraj Patil, was unable to handle it. “Manmohan Singh wanted his best man on the job, that was Chidambaram,” Varma said. “That meant the finance ministry was now empty.” {010-S11}

Singh would have taken Finance himself, but he had to have an operation that January. Sonia Gandhi put Pranab Mukherjee in the post, a socialist thinker, Varma said, from the Indira 70s. Retrospective taxation followed, and around 2013 Mukherjee was kicked upstairs to the presidency.
~ Chidambaram returned. After 2014 the Jaitley ministry showed continuity for a while, then politics took over: from 2015, Varma said, “everything goes to hell”.
stories.why: Ajay Shah rejected the bad-luck story. A chain of accidents can derail an economy only if everything depends on who sits in which chair, he argued; the answer is to write freedom into laws and organisation design. {010-C13}

quiz.q: Which waterway, opened in 1869, cut the sea route from London to Bombay?
quiz.a: The Suez Canal, sending ships via Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

quiz.q: Why, by Amit Varma’s account, did ice factories spring up in the American Midwest?
quiz.a: Malaria in India meant quinine, tonic water, gin and tonic, and so ice.

quiz.q: Who, according to Ajay Shah, introduced the world’s first capital controls?
quiz.a: Adolf Hitler, in Germany; before 1914 nobody needed passports either.

quiz.q: What did Nehru tell J.R.D. Tata about profit, as Varma quoted it?
quiz.a: “Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.”

quiz.q: Which three Gujaratis became India’s most powerful people in 1977?
quiz.a: Morarji Desai, H.M. Patel and D.T. Lakdawala, under the Janata government.

quiz.q: Why did the finance ministry fall empty after the 2008 Mumbai attacks?
quiz.a: Manmohan Singh moved P. Chidambaram to Home to replace Shivraj Patil.
